title: My post
hookLine: stay at the post you've been given, like a soldier

cards: It's three in the morning. A night nurse is the only person awake on the ward. Nothing is happening.
Nobody will thank her for the next four hours, and if she wandered off a while, maybe no one would notice. She stays. She walks the hall, checks the monitors, refills a water cup.
A lighthouse keeper once did the same, and a soldier at a gate, and a parent sitting up with a fever. Epictetus had a word for that kind of staying.
It comes from the army, and it's in book three, chapter twenty-four, again.

teach.b: Each person's life, Epictetus says, is a kind of military service, long and varied. In an army not everyone does the same job. One stands guard, one goes out to scout, one goes into battle.
Not everyone can stay in one spot, and it wouldn't be better if they did. Each has a post.

What ruins a soldier, he says, is grumbling at the general's orders: why me, why here, why the night shift. If everyone did that, nothing would get done; the camp wouldn't be guarded, the trench wouldn't be dug.
The Stoics believed a reason runs through the whole of things, which they sometimes called God or Zeus, and that your post is part of it.
The picture goes back to Plato's account of Socrates on trial, a speech Epictetus quotes elsewhere in the Discourses.

Socrates told the jury that wherever a person has been stationed, they should stay and face the danger, as he had as a soldier in three battles, and as he would now at the post of philosophy, even if it cost his life.
Look at what we gathered this week: alone, not lonely; a scout; in its season; at home here; free is wanting rightly; nothing to take.
And now my post. Your post may be a cash register, a crib, a classroom, a hospital bed you're lying in. It's still a post.

how: Stoics often describe their daily responsibilities as a post they've been assigned, and try to carry them out fully and without complaint, wherever they happen to be.

o: a letter or message you send to a friend
the station in life where you're placed to serve
a job you picked for its pay and status

p: stayed at his post on trial

s: Epictetus thought everyone should have the same job
in his army one guards, one scouts, one fights; each has a different post.
the post image goes back to Socrates at his trial
in Plato's Apology Socrates says a person should stay where they've been stationed.
Socrates had served as a soldier
he told the jury he had held his post in three battles.

games.q: you're Socrates, on trial. the jury will let you go if you stop doing philosophy in the streets. what do you say?
o: say you'll stay at the post you were given, as you did in battle.
games.why: in Plato's Apology he says he won't desert his post, just as he didn't in battle, even if it costs his life. it did.

practice: Sit up a little, like someone on watch, and name plainly your post for today: the meeting, the kid you're picking up, the shift, the long recovery.
Notice any grumbling that comes with it, the why me, and set it down beside you like a heavy bag. Breathe, and feel yourself standing where you've been put, steady, eyes open.

wordCard.voice: My post. Epictetus' soldier: each life has its own station, guard or scout or fighter, and the work is to stay at it well. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an arrangement, a soldier's place in the line; the word for a post or station.

carryVoice: Your line: stay at it well. Guard, scout or fighter, each one has a post. Day four hundred twenty-seven, and the end of a week.
